name: Rhyme-as-Reason Effect
description: Statements phrased in rhyme can feel truer or more valid than semantically equivalent non-rhyming versions. The verbal form itself gets mistaken for evidence.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to UX writing, slogans, trust copy, error messages, and assistant phrasing: rhyming microcopy can sound wiser or more trustworthy than plain-language alternatives with the same meaning.
prevalence_note: A well-known named finding in persuasion/copywriting and cognitive-bias roundups, but not a baseline day-to-day UX law on the level of anchoring, defaults, or social proof.

findings.description: Participants rated unfamiliar aphorisms as more accurate when they were presented in rhyming form than when they were presented as semantically equivalent non-rhyming paraphrases, even though the two versions were judged equally comprehensible.
findings.source_title: The Keats heuristic: Rhyme as reason in aphorism interpretation

findings.description: Three experiments testing newly-created advertising slogans found rhyming versions rated as more likeable, original, memorable, campaign-suitable, persuasive, and trustworthy than non-rhyming equivalents in a between-subjects design. The effect initially appeared weaker for social-advertising messages than commercial ones, but this difference disappeared when participants directly compared rhymes and non-rhymes within-subjects -- rhymes were then clearly preferred across both ad types on both form and content ratings. An independent replication extending the rhyme-as-reason effect from the original aphorism paradigm into real advertising-slogan content, with an honest design-sensitive nuance (weaker in between-subjects comparison, robust in within-subjects comparison) rather than a uniformly clean effect.
findings.source_title: Rhyme as reason in commercial and social advertising.
